episodes.167687: Mild and rather moist lower levels combined with an approaching, weakening cold front to generate numerous early afternoon thunderstorms across central Indiana.  Given the weak flow and low-shear environment, most storms were single-cellular with a very slow southerly storm motion.  Amid scattered heavy rainfall rates were a couple reports of marginally large hail between Indianapolis and Bloomington.
episodes.168079: Pre frontal trough moved across the forecast area, interacting with a semi unstable and low shear environment to bring cluster of showers and storms to the area. Many of the storms produced sub severe hail.
episodes.168446: Scattered thunderstorms moved across northwest Illinois during the evening of May 13th.
episodes.168482: A weak frontal boundary tracked through the area along with a weak upper level disturbance combined with daytime heating to produce strong thunderstorms during the late afternoon and evening hours on Friday (5/13). The strongest storms produced hail up to nickel size across portions of north-central and east-central Wisconsin.
episodes.168668: Several waterspouts developed in association with a mature cumulus congestus cloud line near the lower Florida Keys.
episodes.168711: Northern Ohio resided in the warm sector as a surface trough axis moved generally eastward through the region during the afternoon and early evening of the 14th. Low-level convergence and ascent along the trough axis acted as a focus for the development of isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms. This convection occurred in an environment comprised of weak to moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, respectively, and weak effective bulk shear. Several single cell thunderstorms managed to produce small to marginally-severe hail and/or damaging wind gusts. Slow moving thunderstorms caused isolated flash flooding, with rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches in one hour.
episodes.168848: A line of thunderstorms moved through southwest North Dakota in an environment of modest instability and weak deep layer shear. One storm produced wind gusts of 63 mph at the Dickinson Airport in Stark County.
episodes.168996: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the morning hours of May 14th across portions of Southwest Arkansas, near a weak surface frontal boundary that was stationary across this area into Eastern Arkansas. A weak shortwave trough shifted east atop this boundary after sunrise, enhancing large scale forcing along the boundary as it tapped available instability along and to the south. This combination resulted in an isolated severe thunderstorm developing over Northeast Hempstead and Northern Nevada Counties in Southwest Arkansas, where quarter size hail fell just south of Prescott before weakening shortly thereafter.
episodes.169077: A cold front moved through the region triggering thunderstorms. Some of the storms became severe with numerous reports of large hail.
episodes.169079: Storms developed along a weak frontal boundary across the southern half of the forecast area. Some of the storms became severe with several reports of large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.169212: A leftover outflow boundary sparked a few thunderstorms across the Missouri Bootheel during the early evening hours on May 14, 2022 resulting in large hail.
episodes.169270: A weak cold front moved across the state, resulting in a few showers and thunderstorms. While most remained sub-severe, one thunderstorm produced a gust of 57 knots as dry air helped to enhance evaporative cooling.
episodes.169329: On May 14th, a cold front stalled in Northwestern Kansas during the afternoon hours. Due to this stalled cold front, thunderstorms developed within the region. One of these thunderstorms became severe and yielded hail up to a quarter in size.
episodes.169381: High cloud base showers produced a local microburst that downed 4 trees near Jenny Lake. One tree was 20 inches in diameter.
episodes.169406: A few severe storms produced large hail and strong winds across portions of south central Kansas on the 13th of May.
episodes.169426: Isolated supercells produce very large hail over portions of north central Kansas the evening of May 14th. Isolated thunderstorms developed along Highway 283 in northern Kansas around 3 PM CDT, then moved east. This activity quickly developed into supercells, with several of these cells ultimately splitting into both left and right movers. Deep layer wind shear on this day favored right-moving supercells to be most dominant. One of the strongest supercells on this day split over Norton County about 3:30 PM CDT, with the right-mover turning southeast into western Phillips County about 30 minutes later. Very large hail was the primary threat, and golf ball to baseball sized hail was reported. This same cell, along with another cell arriving from the west, also tracked across Rooks County while likely maintaining severe strength, but no large hail reports were received. This activity ultimately weakened and dissipated between 5:30-6:30 PM CDT over Rooks and Osborne Counties.
episodes.169561: An isolated severe thunderstorm developed near Tecumseh.
episodes.169585: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed across west central Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 14th. The strongest storms produced large hail to half dollar size. Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms redeveloped late in the evening across northwestern Arkansas. Moderately strong instability combined with strong deep layer wind shear promoted the development of a supercell in Washington County, which produced large hail up to ping pong ball size.||Thunderstorms that developed across northeastern Kansas during the early morning hours of the 15th, moved southeast across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the afternoon. Additional thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening near the outflow boundary from these storms. The strongest storms produced large hail up to quarter size and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.169620: Strong to severe thunderstorms with heavy rainfall impacted the region from the afternoon into early evening. Isolated flooding occurred where rainfall was heaviest.
episodes.169621: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms with heavy rainfall impacted the region during the afternoon and evening as an unstable airmass and upper level disturbances interacted with a stalled outflow boundary. Several locations along and east of a line from Lake of the Ozarks to Marshfield to Branson reported hail of quarter to golf ball size.
episodes.169627: Heavy rainfall from 2 to 3 inches from May 8 to May 12 across northeast into east central portions of South Dakota resulted in a brief period of minor flooding along the upper portions of the Big Sioux River.
episodes.169786: Scattered clusters of showers and thunderstorms developed in the afternoon hours ahead of a weakening stationary front oriented north to south across the lower Midwest. Storms fed off of diurnal instability and gradually moved southward from southern Indiana into the Louisville metro, where they intensified enough to cause scattered wind damage. Minor flooding occurred as a result of heavy rainfall in Franklin County.
episodes.169841: For much of the state, May 13th was the end of the heatwave as a cold front moved into the area and showers and thunderstorms developed. Thunderstorms were most widespread on the 15th with several reports of hail as large as golf balls and numerous wind damage reports. A wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at the Jacksonville/LR Air Force Base.||Some relief (cooler air) came on the 15th in the form of a cold front. At the same time, there were strong to severe storms ahead of the front.  Storms were sure to thrive given an enormous amount of energy in place. Models showed a line of storms traversing the region from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and these were expected to unleash strong to damaging winds. Updrafts into some storms were likely to be powerful enough to suspend hailstones aloft, and allow them to grow. So, very large hail was possible. There were already a few hailstorms on the 14th, with lime size hail at Jasper (Newton County), and golf ball size hail at Harrison (Boone County). Tornadoes were much less likely because steering winds were generally weak (30 knots or less), and there was not much shear.||Between 1100 am and 1200 pm CST, a large cluster of storms arrived from Missouri. Ahead of the cluster, isolated to scattered storms erupted mainly north and west of Little Rock (Pulaski County). Golf ball size hail was reported at Boxley (Newton County) and the west side of Russellville (Pope County). There was half dollar size hail at London and just north of Russellville (both in Pope County), and quarter size stones at Chickalah (Yell County), Nimrod (Perry County), and Paris (Logan County).||As the afternoon progressed, the cluster of storms worked from northwest into central and southeast Arkansas. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, with some trees on houses. At least 50,000 power outages were noted at one point. At Russellville (Pope County), a tree fell on a vehicle, and two people had to be extricated and taken to the hospital. A tree also came down on a travel trailer close to Hazen (Prairie County). Fallen trees blocked Highway 7 near Fourche Junction (Perry County), Highway 46 at Sheridan (Grant County), and Highway 54 at Sulphur Springs (Jefferson County). Roads were blocked by trees at a campground northeast of Fifty Six (Stone County). A roof was blown off of a storage building west of Hot Springs (Garland County).||There was a 58 mph gust at the Little Rock Air Force Base (Pulaski County), a 56 mph gust at McCreanor (Lonoke County), a 55 mph gust at Little Rock National Airport (Pulaski County), and a 54 mph gust at the Stuttgart Airport in Fairmount (Prairie County).
episodes.170011: A warm front and dryline intersection was better defined by the afternoon north of I-20. Also, strong instability was in the area. As a result, isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and early evening across mainly the Big Country. A few storms became severe and produced large hail. Also, localized wind damage was reported near Lake Brownwood. The San Angelo ASOS reported a wind gust near 75 mph on May 10th.
episodes.170020: Showers and thunderstorms developed over the Big Country along a dryline, and over Northwest Texas near a stationary front, the afternoon of Friday May 13. Some of these storms became severe as they moved into western and northwestern portions of the forecast area Friday evening. Strong to damaging wind gusts developed farther east later in the evening due to heat burst winds associated with dissipating thunderstorms.
episodes.170056: A slow-moving cold front interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms across west-central Illinois during the late afternoon and early evening of May 13th.  One of the strongest cells within the line dropped golf ball-sized hail near Brooklyn in Schuyler County.  Other storms produced excessive rainfall rates that led to minor flash flooding across portions of Schuyler and Fulton Counties.
episodes.170058: A cold front interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered scattered strong thunderstorms across east-central and southeast Illinois during the afternoon and early evening of May 14th. Hail as large as nickels was reported near the town of Casey in Clark County.
episodes.170171: A series of short waves affected the region during the 14th and 15th producing rounds of storms. An isolated thunderstorm became severe on both days.
episodes.170189: A severe thunderstorm developed over Baldwin County and produced large hail.
episodes.170203: Isolated supercells developed during the evening of the 13th and moved southward across northern Oklahoma. Many large hail reports were received.
episodes.170279: A surface trough across the area along with sea breezes led to the development of scattered strong thunderstorms over parts of South Florida.
episodes.170325: Marginal boundary layer moisture along combined with sufficient daytime warming was enough to generate mainly high based thunderstorms. Ample shear of over 30 kts and CAPE values over 1000 J/kg contributed to a number of nickel to quarter sized hail reports.
episodes.170353: Isolated supercells brought numerous hail reports to the Wichita Falls area during the evening of the 13th.
episodes.170356: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 14th across central Texas, with a few storms moving northward into western north Texas where large hail was reported.
episodes.176066: Heavy rain occurred in portions of northeast Kentucky on May 14, leading to swollen creeks and streams across the area. While no flash flood reports were received, there was a fatality reported in Rowan County. According to the county EM and rescue squad, an 80-year-old man was on a utility vehicle with his wife, attempting to cross a swollen creek along Bullfork Road. The utility vehicle reportedly got stuck, and the man got off the vehicle and into the high waters to free the vehicle and get to the other side. The current of the water knocked him off his feet, and he was swept away down the creek. Rescue workers were able to get to him, and take him to a nearby medical center - however, he was later pronounced dead.

Stark County Sheriff and North Canton Police reported flash flooding across North Canton. River levels on Zimber Ditch and West Branch Nimishillen Creek rose 5.5 feet in one hour, reaching flood stage by 730 PM EDT. Flood waters from Zimber Ditch entered businesses along Whipple Avenue NW. Reports of more than one dozen homes with several feet of water into basements throughout North Canton. Per local media, county officials estimated the number of homes and businesses impacted by flooding was in the hundreds.  Radar estimated rainfall totals of 2.5 to 4 inches fell in the northern portion of North Canton in one hour, with peak instantaneous rainfall rates of 5 to 6 inches per hour.
